grade.basis: Cello 1 (40126.pdf) moves between bass, tenor and treble clef and sits in upper and thumb positions (thumb signs, p.3, 9, 10-11). The No.6 Allegro (pp.10-11) has long runs of 16th notes across strings and shifts into treble clef, with trills and some double stops; the other five pieces are mostly lyrical in first to fourth position (pp.2, 7-9). Cello 2 (40127.pdf pp.1-3) is simpler, in bass clef with repeated chords and 8ths. Ensemble demands are ordinary (cello 1 leads, 2 and 3 accompany).

The PDF (267987.pdf) holds the four separate violin parts but only No.1 Andante-Allegro of the four pieces, so the other three pieces were not seen. Violin 1 (PDF pp.3-5) stays in first to third position (top note about a high C), with simple 8th and quarter-note rhythms, a few trills, scale runs, occasional double stops and dynamic contrast in B-flat major. Violins 2 and 4 (PDF pp.7-8, 15-17) are easier still, with long rests and accompanying figures. Ensemble demands are light (shared rhythms, homophonic).

Cello 1 (44907.pdf pp.2-3, 8-11) is written mostly in tenor and treble clef and lives in thumb and upper positions with fingerings up to 4, sustained high lines, long slurred 8th-note runs, chromatic runs and trills, plus a brilliante Finale (Allegro agitato) with fast leaps across strings and key changes. Cello 3 (44909.pdf pp.2-4) is a bass-clef accompaniment with pizzicato and sustained notes, which is moderate. The first cello carries the demand; ensemble balance is straightforward.

This is a full score of a four-movement suite (44997.pdf, PDF pp.3-18 inspected in part). The writing is densely chromatic and rhythmically independent: fast 16th-note passages with accidentals on nearly every note (PDF pp.8-9), long trills on the high E string, pizzicato-to-arco switches within a bar (PDF p.5), and constant alternation of 16th figures between all three parts. The Allegro vivace finale (PDF pp.15-18) layers chromatic 8th-note lines in all parts with rapid entries, so intonation and ensemble coordination are the main difficulty rather than pure speed.

Cello 1 (45425.pdf pp.2-5) alternates bass, tenor and alto clef, with thumb-position sign and fingerings up to 4 in high positions, 16th-note turns and trills, rapid string-crossing 8th-note patterns (p.4) and a quick Allegro non troppo at quarter 112. Cello 3 (45427.pdf pp.2-3) is mostly repeated 8ths, pizzicato and sustained bass lines in first to fourth position. The upper part is the early-advanced demand; the ensemble is a classic salon trio with the top cello leading.

Only Dancla's Le Depart, L'Arrivee and Le Retour were graded (465510.pdf pp.2-6 for violin 1, PDF p.27 for violin 4; the Mozart and Schumann pieces in the same PDF were ignored). Violin 1 plays in first to third position, with sautille 16th-note passages, hooked and slurred staccato, trills, tied-note melodies and up to the high E; the March (Le Retour, PDF pp.5-6) is the hardest with its lively dotted and 16th figures in D major. Violin 4 (PDF p.27) is lower, mostly first-position chords and an accompaniment. Ensemble demands are moderate (imitative entries and short solo cues).

A short Adagio of about 45 bars (404072.pdf score PDF pp.3-4; parts in 404073.pdf pp.1-2). Cello 1 is in tenor clef and sits in middle to upper positions, with sustained whole notes, simple slurred 8th-note and quarter-note melody, and one stretch of continuous 16th-note alternating figures (pp.3-4, bars 15-23). Cello 2 is bass clef and plainer; cello 3 has a rocking 16th-note arpeggiated figure, cello 4 steady 8th-note pulses. Rhythms are regular and the ensemble demands low (static harmony).

A five-movement suite in full score (415144.pdf). Cello 1 is written in tenor and treble clef, with chromatic and rising scale runs in the upper positions, a con liberta passage with 16th figures (pp.3-5), 16th-note spiccato and legato passagework in the Scherzo (p.20), and harmonics (pp.20-21). The finale (Allegro con brio, pp.29-30) keeps all four players in fast, overlapping 8th-note lines with frequent clef changes. The top part reaches advanced-level technique, and rhythmic coordination across four equal parts adds some ensemble demand.

Suite No.3 in four movements (415146.pdf, parts for Cello I, III, IV). Cello 1 reads alto/tenor and treble clef throughout with thumb position, natural and artificial harmonics and octave-displaced harmonics at the end of the Vivo (PDF p.5), rapid detache 8th-note arpeggios across strings (PDF pp.5-6), repeated double-stop figures on the last page of that movement and a high-register melody in the Andante (PDF p.3). Cello 3 (PDF pp.16-17) and Cello 4 (pp.24-26) are mainly pizzicato chords, long notes and tuplet figures in bass clef, with some tenor-clef excursions. The ensemble is well balanced, with some tricky triplet-against-duplet coordination in the Andantino.

Three pieces in 465514.pdf: Elfenreigen (Scherzo, PDF pp.2-6 score and parts), Abend (PDF pp.17-19) and Nachtzauber (PDF pp.28-30, violin 1). Elfenreigen is largely first position, light 3/4 with slurred 8ths, trills and plain slurred and detached bowing; Abend has chromatic part-writing with position changes (II-IV markings). Nachtzauber is the hardest: violin 1 sustains long high-register lines on the E string (fingered 4s and high-position notes with many ledger lines), a gentle pp entry and wide dynamic swells (PDF pp.29-30). Other parts are mostly long notes in first to third position. The ensemble demand is in balance and intonation of four sustained, chromatic parts.

Introduction et Polacca for four violins concertants (592377.pdf is an engraved full score, 534302.pdf the 19th-century violin parts). Violin 1 plays an Andante introduction with sustained high E-string notes (fingered up to 4 in 5th-position territory, PDF p.1 of 534302), then a Polacca in A major with spiccato 16th-note flourishes marked 'Sp.' and 'Fr.' (tip and heel), ricochet-style leggiero groups, trills (592377 pp.4-6, 10-11), rapid pizzicato-to-arco switches, and fast triplet and 16th-note scale runs in the coda (p.11). Middle section in D major (pp.8-9) is calmer. The ensemble must trade quick motifs among all four players, which pushes it slightly above the notes alone.

Seven short exercises in a clean engraved score (541895.pdf). All four parts are in bass clef and stay in first to fourth position (cello 1 rises only to about the G or A just above the bass staff, mostly in whole and half notes, PDF pp.1-3, 18-19). Rhythm is quarter notes, half notes and simple 8th-note patterns (PDF pp.4-6, 25-27), repeated 8th-note ostinato in cellos 3 and 4, a few slurs and light staccato. Key signatures stay at up to three flats and two sharps; ensemble demands are minimal (all parts move together in block chords).

Consort No.1 in three movements (606686.pdf). The Toccata (PDF pp.1-5, 'Virtuoso', quarter 100) is non-stop chromatic 16th-note runs with accidentals on nearly every note, entering in canon through all four parts with wide leaps and rapid string crossings. The finale (PDF pp.13-15, 'Virtuoso', dotted quarter 150 in 6/8) has chromatic 16th-note cells in broken rhythms and fast accompanying figures. Positions stay mostly first to third on the E string, but the speed, chromatic intonation and canon entries are demanding. Floating (PDF pp.7-8) is a slow legato chorale with tricky tuning, and Pulse (PDF p.9) uses repeated 8th double stops under pp dynamics, so the ensemble demand on top of the notes is modest.

entries.heldReason: Neither PDF contains the stated piece for the stated scoring. 702415.pdf is a four-cello set of only two pieces (Religioso and Nocturne, titled '2 Morceaux de Salon', cello 1 and 2 parts only, no opus number visible), and 925426.pdf is the Op.53 Nocturne for cello and piano or harmonium, so the four-piece Op.53 set for four cellos is not present. Musically the two four-cello pieces are slow, lyrical, mostly in bass and tenor clef with some treble clef in cello 1, long legato lines in middle and upper positions and simple rhythms, so they are well within a moderate, intermediate-to-upper-intermediate range, but no grade is assigned to the stated four-piece work.

grade.basis: A three-movement contemporary score (872943.pdf, 2006). Movement I (Elegiaco, PDF pp.3-9) has long sustained lines in tenor and alto clef, molto vibrato and sul ponticello, with cello 2 repeatedly entering on very high harmonic or flautando notes above the treble staff and cello 3 on pizzicato ostinato. Movement II (Animando, PDF pp.10-20) has continuous 16th-note chromatic ostinati, rapid 16th triplet figuration in the upper register (PDF pp.17-19), long trills, col legno, sul pont tremolo, pizzicato and sudden shifts between 4/4, 5/4 and 2/4. Movement III (Semplice, PDF pp.21-23) uses clef changes mid-phrase, high flautando harmonics and mixed meters. The notes alone are around early-diploma level and the independence of parts, mixed meters and extended techniques add ensemble demands.

Four pieces in a full score (1009520.pdf: Song Without Words, an Allegretto/Scherzo-type piece, Andante in E-flat, and March). Cello 1 is almost always in tenor clef with excursions into treble clef and constant upper-position playing (PDF pp.1-6, 28-31, 40-43), but the rhythms are simple: lyrical 8th-note slurs, triplet 8ths and light staccato, and the fastest passages are 8th-note runs (PDF pp.40-43, 60-63, 72-75). Tessitura reaches the high A and above in the March coda (PDF p.75). Cellos 2-4 are bass clef, much easier. Ensemble demands are mild: the lower three play homophonic accompaniments with occasional imitation.

Parts only (10005.pdf: cello 1 PDF pp.4-6, viola/cello 2 PDF p.8-9, cello 4 PDF pp.20-22). Cello 1 is mainly alto and tenor clef with excursions into treble, sits in the upper positions throughout, and has 16th-note slurred figures, harmonic flageolets (Scherzo trio, 'Sul G. Flag.') and thumb-position scale passages (Introduzione and Moderato finale, PDF pp.4-6, with fingerings up to 4 and positions II-VII marked). The writing is lyrical with few extended technical demands. Cello 4 is bass clef with long pedal notes and some pizzicato-arco switches. The ensemble is a real quartet with imitative entries but balanced difficulty.

A theme with variations in a notation-program score (source42-617255.pdf). Cello 1 reads bass, tenor and alto clef in alternation and plays in upper positions with fluent 16th-note runs and turns (PDF pp.1-6), 6/8, 2/4 and 3/4 contrasts, a Maestoso with chordal figures (PDF p.9), an Andantino and a Scherzando in 6/8 (PDF pp.10-12), and ending on sustained dynamics (PDF p.17). The material is regular and imitative; the tenor-clef upper register and the sixteenth runs are the highest hurdle for cello 1, so it sits at the early advanced end with ordinary ensemble demands.

Single-movement Elegie in an engraved full score plus viola parts (source42-10006.pdf, PDF pp.2-3, 5-6). Cello 1 is in tenor clef in a high but moderate register (up to about C or D above the staff), mainly slurred quarter and 8th-note phrases, a few short 16th-note groups and a short chromatic passage, with the Allegro moderato in D major quite regular. Cello 4 has a short rising 16th-note run in positions 1-4 (PDF p.3, bottom staves) and pizzicato bass. The main demands are tenor-clef reading, intonation and phrasing, with the Meno mosso section requiring balance across four equal voices.

A single 3/8 Scherzo (source42-103548.pdf, Violin I PDF pp.1-3; handwritten score source42-103546.pdf pp.1-6, 14-16). Violin 1 plays fast repeated 16th-note patterns marked ff and fff, with whole bars of slurred repeated notes (PDF pp.1-3) written on four or more ledger lines above the staff, and a closing stretch of about 40 bars of continuous high-register 16ths ending on sustained very high notes. The part also contains long stretches of metrically displaced rests and rapid chromatic cells. The lower parts (handwritten score) use dense 16th-note repeated-note ostinati and pitch-displaced figures. Extreme high-position security and endurance plus tight rhythmic interlock are what lift it. The handwritten score is hard to read, so some details are inferred from the engraved Violin I part.

Gavotte in D major, Moderato 2/4 (source42-82715.pdf, Violin I PDF pp.2-3 and Violin II p.5). Violin 1 stays in first and third position with a top note around B above the staff, uses short 16th-note groups, dotted and grace-note figures, simple slurred scales and accented quarter notes, plus a short G major trio in the same range. Violin 2 is lower and simpler, with held and detached 8ths in first position. The parts are mostly homophonic with the same rhythms across voices, so ensemble demands are modest.

Three-movement quartet score (503799.pdf), headed 'for ensemble classes and auditions'. Violin 1 is mostly in first to fifth position (PDF pp.1-3, 5), with 16th-note scale runs, a 6-tuplet flourish and a saltellato bowing in the Allegretto (PDF pp.4-5), pizzicato-arco alternation, many chromatic accidentals and constant key-area shifts in 3/8. The Finale (PDF p.8) climbs to repeated high notes four or more ledger lines above the staff with ff dynamics and fast 16ths with grace-note ornaments. The lower parts are in first to third position and handle pizzicato offbeats against bowed lines, adding some ensemble coordination.
